prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which established the basis for incretin-based therapy of type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: GLP-1 is the one candidate that all six of us placed in our top three, and that convergence reflects substance rather than habit. The chain from gut-hormone physiology (the incretin effect, proglucagon processing, the truncated active peptide GLP-1(7-36)) to a drug class that reduces glycaemia, body weight and cardiovascular and renal events is mechanistically coherent, independently confirmed over three decades and now backed by very large randomized outcome trials. It is original, it is a physiological discovery in the sense of the Nobel will, and its benefit to patients is broad and durable. A physiology-led trio of Holst, Drucker and Mojsov credits the people who established what the hormone is and does, which is what a discovery prize should reward.
statement.case_against: The attribution is genuinely fragile. Mojsov's role in identifying the active peptide is contested relative to Habener, who is not among the credited names, and any trio that leaves out Knudsen omits the person who designed the long-acting analogues that actually became medicines. If the Committee reads the discovery as the drug rather than the hormone, my trio is the wrong trio. There is also a risk that an obesity and diabetes prize is read as celebrating a commercial product, and we cannot add names that are not on the ballot to repair the credit.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks the unfolded protein response first as a conceptually complete, mature signalling discovery (Walter and Mori), and puts GLP-1 third with Knudsen in the trio, noting that Mojsov's role is disputed.
responses.response: I agree that the UPR is a clean, textbook-level two-person discovery and I would not object to it, which is why I keep it as an alternative. I do not think its disease relevance is yet at the level of GLP-1: as I read it, that evidence is still largely correlative or preclinical, whereas incretin biology has demonstrated human benefit. On Knudsen I qualify rather than dismiss your view. Her work on acylated analogues is the step that made the hormone usable, but it is industrial drug design built on the physiology that Holst and Drucker established, and the Committee has usually preferred to honour the discovery of the principle. I would only accept Knudsen in place of Mojsov if the credit review shows that Mojsov's priority for the active peptide cannot be defended.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks GLP-1 first with Drucker, Holst and Knudsen as a coherent physiology-to-therapy trio, and ranks TNF blockade third.
responses.response: We agree on the discovery and differ on the third name. A trio that runs from physiology (Holst), mechanism and translation (Drucker) to drug design (Knudsen) tells a tidy story, but it leaves the identification of the active peptide form unrecognised, and without GLP-1(7-36) the physiology has no defined molecular agent. I think that omission is harder to defend than leaving out an industrial developer. I recognise this rests on my own reading of a contested priority record that I cannot verify here, so I would want the attribution review to settle it before the final ballot. I also note that TNF blockade, which you favour, is not on the shortlist, so I cannot weigh it in this round.

responses.point: The chair ranks GLP-1 first with the same trio I propose, then CAR-T second and antisense correction of SMN2 for spinal muscular atrophy third, valuing the clear mechanism-to-therapy path of nusinersen as a neurologist.
responses.response: I share your preference for prizes with a defined molecular mechanism leading to treatment, and nusinersen fits that. My reservation is the size and breadth of the effect. Spinal muscular atrophy is a rare disease, and the credit would also have to deal with the SMN1 gene discovery by Melki, Lefebvre and Dreyfuss, who are not on this ballot, so the prize would sit on a partly incomplete discovery chain. As a motor-system scientist I take the clinical transformation seriously, and I would rank it ahead of the UPR on patient impact alone, but I do not think it displaces GLP-1 or CAR-T.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks GLP-1 first and the UPR second, treating Mojsov's identification of the active peptide as decisive but contested, and notes that Knudsen could be an alternative to Mojsov.
responses.response: I agree with your handling of Mojsov and Knudsen as the real fork in the attribution. Where I would push back is on treating them as interchangeable: Mojsov's contribution is to the discovery of the active molecule, while Knudsen's is to drug design, so the choice is really about whether we are crediting a discovery or a development. I would resolve that in favour of discovery, but I would not call it a clear-cut resolution.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks GLP-1 first and optogenetics (Deisseroth, Nagel, Hegemann) second, as a general-purpose method now reaching clinical use in vision restoration.
responses.response: Optogenetics matters a great deal to my own field and I would be wary of letting that raise its ranking. It is a method invention with a medical dimension that is still small, and the six credited people force exclusions of Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck that I cannot justify within a three-person limit. I would put it behind GLP-1 and CAR-T, and I would not favour it as a second prize part unless the committee wants a methods-oriented achievement.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen is the better third name depends on a priority question (Mojsov, Habener, Holst) that I cannot resolve from the evidence supplied.
Whether a prize split between GLP-1 physiology and CAR-T, with at most three people in all, is feasible without sacrificing credit in one of them.
Whether the Committee wants to treat the discovery of the hormone's physiology or the drug that came from it as the prizeworthy achievement.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My documented collaborations (Grillner, Ernfors, and a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons) do not involve any credited name on the shortlist.
